segments.text_en: The arrow that cannot move. Section 1 — Zeno's Arrow "At every instant, the arrow occupies a fixed position. A thing in a fixed position is at rest. So when does it move?" — Zeno of Elea, c. 450 BC The paradox haunted Western thought for over two thousand years. Aristotle tried to refute it. He failed. So did everyone else — until Newton and Leibniz, in the late 1600s, discovered the answer. Don't ask what the arrow does at a single instant. Instead, look at two nearby moments, measure how far the arrow moves between them, and divide by the time elapsed. Then shrink that gap . The ratio settles to a definite number — the instantaneous velocity. The arrow was never frozen. We just needed the right way to see it. Try it on the right. Drag Δt toward zero and watch.

segments.text_en: Can you beat a 330-year-old curve?. Section 3 — The Brachistochrone Race In June 1696, Johann Bernoulli posed a challenge to Europe's mathematicians: what curve carries a bead from A to B in the least time under gravity? Newton received the problem at 4 pm, solved it by 4 am, and sent the solution anonymously. Bernoulli recognized him anyway: "I know the lion by its claw." The answer is a cycloid — the curve traced by a point on a rolling wheel. It dips steeply, gaining speed before straightening out. It looks reckless. It always wins. segments.text_en: How to measure the unmeasurable. Section 4 — Filling the Gap Archimedes could find the area under a parabola — but it took him a lifetime of ingenuity. Riemann's idea, twenty-one centuries later, was almost rude in its simplicity: chop the region into thin rectangles and add up their areas. The thinner the slices, the better the answer. segments.text_en: Some infinities fit. Section 5 — The Infinite Staircase Add 1 + ½ + ⅓ + ¼ + … forever. The sum grows without bound — slowly, but inexorably. The tower has no ceiling. This is the harmonic series , and its divergence stunned 14th-century mathematicians. Now try 1 + ¼ + ⅑ + ⁄ + … — the reciprocals of perfect squares. The tower stops. It converges. And it converges to exactly π/6. Why should π — the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter — appear in a sum of fractions? Euler solved this in 1735 and it made him famous across Europe. segments.text_en: Everything moves. The question was never whether, but how — and the answer turned out to be a limit, a slope, a curve you sculpt with your own hand. A ball on a hill. A bead on a wire that always loses to a 330-year-old cycloid. Rectangles that dissolve into area. Blocks that somehow stack to π. This is calculus — the mathematics of change, of motion, of everything that refuses to stand still.
segments.text_ko: 모든 것은 움직인다. 문제는 움직이느냐가 아니라 어떻게 움직이느냐였고 — 그 답은 극한, 기울기, 당신이 직접 빚은 곡선이었습니다. 언덕 위의 공. 330년 된 사이클로이드에 항상 지는 구슬. 넓이 속으로 녹아드는 직사각형들. 어쩐지 π로 쌓이는 블록들. 이것이 미적분학입니다 — 변화의 수학, 운동의 수학, 결코 가만히 있지 않는 모든 것의 수학.
